reason: The picture shows the intersections as crossings, which curve is on top, and why the area is curve minus line.

scenes.title: Why the area is curve minus line
scenes.purpose: See that $C$ is above $l$ between the crossings at $x=1$ and $x=6$, so the area is the integral of (curve $-$ line), and that the area reaches $\frac{125}{6}$.

steps.text: Setting $-x^2+8x-5=x+1$ gives $x^2-7x+6=0$, so $(x-1)(x-6)=0$. The line crosses the curve at $A$ and $B$, where $x=1$ and $x=6$. This is the M1 for forming and solving the quadratic, and the A1 for the two roots.

Check $x=2$: the dashed segment runs from $3$ on the line up to $7$ on the curve, so $C$ is above $l$ between the crossings. The integrand is (curve $-$ line) $=-x^2+7x-6$. Integrating it is the M1. Turning it round to line $-$ curve gives $-\frac{125}{6}$.

Drag $k$ from $1$ up to $6$. The shaded area is $\left[-\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{7x^2}{2}-6x\right]_1^k$, and it closes at the second crossing. Use upper minus lower: $18-\left(-\frac{17}{6}\right)$. This is the dM1. Reversing the limits gives $-\frac{17}{6}-18$.

The area is $\frac{108}{6}+\frac{17}{6}=\frac{125}{6}$, which is the A1*. The orange region is the whole area under $C$ from $1$ to $6$, which is $\frac{130}{3}$. If you integrate only the curve you include the trapezium under $l$, which is $\frac{45}{2}$, and $\frac{130}{3}-\frac{45}{2}=\frac{125}{6}$.

guide.what_you_see: The curve $C$ and the line $l$ from the question, meeting at $A(1, 2)$ and $B(6, 7)$, with the region $R$ between them shaded up to a slider value $k$. A larger pale region under $C$ can also be shown for comparison.

legend.meaning: The left intersection point $(1, 2)$ of $C$ and $l$, where $x=1$ is a root of $x^2-7x+6=0$.
The right intersection point $(6, 7)$ of $C$ and $l$, where $x=6$ is the other root.
The pale orange region between $C$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=6$. Its area is $\frac{130}{3}$, which includes the trapezium under $l$ as well as $R$.
The region between $C$ and $l$ from $x=1$ to $x=k$. At $k=6$ it is the whole region $R$ of the question, with area $\frac{125}{6}$.
A point you can drag along $C$, to compare the height of the curve with the height of the line at the same $x$.
A dashed vertical segment at $x=2$ from the line (height $3$) up to the curve (height $7$), which checks that $C$ is above $l$.

interact.do: Drag the slider from $1$ up to $6$ in steps of $0.1$ to move the right-hand edge of the shaded region $R$.
interact.watch: The shaded region widens and the 'Area so far' reading rises from $0$. At $k=6$ it closes at $B$ and reads $\frac{125}{6}\approx 20.8$.

interact.do: Drag $Q$ along $C$ between $A$ and $B$, that is for $x$ from $1$ to $6$.
interact.watch: $Q$ stays above $l$ for every $x$ in this range. So the integrand is curve minus line, $-x^2+7x-6$, which is positive. At $x=2$, $Q$ sits at the top of the dashed segment, at height $7$.

question_link.text: $C$ and $l$ are the curve and line of the question. $A$ and $B$ are the roots $x=1$ and $x=6$ from the M1 and A1 for solving $x^2-7x+6=0$. The shaded $R$ is the region whose area comes from integrating (curve $-$ line), which is the second M1. Substituting the limits $6$ and $1$ is the dM1, and the reading of $\frac{125}{6}$ at $k=6$ is the result the A1* asks you to show.

read_off: 'Area so far' is the area of $R$ from $x=1$ to the current $k$. This is $\left[-\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{7x^2}{2}-6x\right]_1^k$, and it reaches $\frac{125}{6}\approx 20.8$ at $k=6$.
